tier_reason: The README Benchmark tables (Chrome v131, Ryzen 9 7900X) compare hash-wasm 4.10.0 against pure-JS hash libraries (spark-md5, crypto-js, noble-hashes, jsSHA, node-forge, xxhashjs) and other wasm packages; the harness is public in Daninet/hash-wasm-benchmark (src/benchmark/bench.js plus per-algorithm *.worker.js, package.json pins every competitor version) and the wasm build flags are in scripts/Makefile-clang (clang from a pinned Alpine Docker image). Code, compiler, flags and CPU model are all stated.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: clang --target=wasm32 -flto -O3 -nostdlib -fno-builtin -ffreestanding -mexec-model=reactor, wasm-ld --strip-all (scripts/Makefile-clang, identical at tag v4.10.0); the measured 4.10.0 binaries were built in an alpine:3.18.4 Docker image (scripts/Dockerfile at v4.10.0; HEAD now uses alpine:3.20.3), clang version implied by the Alpine release but not printed in the README; WASM SIMD flags commented out. Baselines are JavaScript run by Chrome v131's V8.
corrections.caveats: First-party numbers from the author's benchmark app (Daninet/hash-wasm-benchmark; the live github.io app was not reachable). The harness checks every library's digest against hash-wasm's output during warm-up, calibrates a per-call divisor, then times about 1 s per scenario (bench.js). The README table is for hash-wasm 4.10.0 (the version the benchmark app pins), while the latest release is 4.12.0. Neither Node's native crypto module (OpenSSL) nor the browser's native WebCrypto digest is in the comparison, so this does not show it beats native hashing. The XXHash64 1 MB figure (15 989 MB/s) is about equal to xxhash-wasm 1.0.2 (15 929 MB/s); its win there is only over pure-JS xxhashjs. No WASM SIMD. Project is C compiled to wasm, so it fits the wasm-libraries-and-apps category (baseline: the JS equivalent in-browser) better than assemblyscript-and-wasm-langs.

notes: All claimed figures match the README tables exactly (MD5 850.31 vs spark-md5 171.73 and crypto-js 46.71 MB/s at 1 MB; SHA256 426.16 vs noble-hashes 110.02; SHA3-512 234.40 vs 14.19; XXHash64 15 989 vs xxhashjs 42.26; PBKDF2-SHA512 588 vs crypto-js 29 ops; Argon2id 438 vs argon2-browser 213 ops). Metadata checked: MIT, 1.2k stars, not a fork, last commit 2024-11-19 (stale). Shortcomings: no native-crypto/WebCrypto baseline, XXHash64 ties xxhash-wasm, first-party run; consider a category override to wasm-libraries-and-apps.

tier_reason: The README Performance section compares json-as with V8's built-in JSON.parse/JSON.stringify; the benchmark code is public (assembly/__benches__/*.bench.ts for AS, bench/*.bench.ts for JS, driven by scripts/run-bench.as.sh and scripts/run-bench.js.sh), the compiler and flags are in those scripts (asc ^0.28.18 -O3 --noAssert --uncheckedBehavior always, wasm-opt -O4), the engine is d8 v8 15.1.42 and the CPU is a Ryzen 7 7800X3D. All of code, compiler, flags and CPU model are stated, so A, with harness asymmetries documented below.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: asc (assemblyscript ^0.28.18 in package.json) -O3 --noAssert --uncheckedBehavior always --runtime incremental --enable bulk-memory --exportStart start --exportRuntime (plus --enable simd in SIMD mode), then wasm-opt -O4 -tnh -iit -ifwl -s 0 with bulk-memory/nontrapping-float-to-int/tail-call/sign-ext/mutable-globals enabled (current scripts/run-bench.as.sh); AS modules run under d8 --no-liftoff, JS baselines under d8 --no-liftoff --no-wasm-tier-up --allow-natives-syntax (scripts/run-bench.js.sh); chart footer: v8 15.1.42, commit 0bb47d4, Jul 17 2026. Scripts are read at HEAD; the flags used at 0bb47d4 were not checked.
corrections.caveats: First-party: the benchmark author is the library author. Chart values exist only in images (SVG and PNG on the docs branch, charts/v1.5.0), not in a text table. The JS baseline parses into generic JavaScript objects while json-as parses into typed structs generated at build time, so the work differs. Harness asymmetry: the JS blackbox() in bench/lib/bench.js runs an indirect eval of '%PerformMicrotaskCheckpoint();' on every timed op, while the AS blackbox is a single store/load, which inflates JS per-op time most on the 19-108 byte rows (JS ops there take only about 125-640 ns); the 5.5 kB rows are least affected. Benchmark builds use --noAssert, --uncheckedBehavior always and wasm-opt -tnh/-iit, which drop assertion and trap checks. The JSON.Obj path is lazy by default since v1.5.0 (values parsed on first access, untouched values re-serialized by copying source bytes), so its deserialize and serialize bars (up to 19,968 MB/s) defer work and are not like-for-like; on the 3D Vector row JSON.Obj ties built-in JSON (82 vs 83 MB/s), and the 0 values on the Alphabet and UUIDv4 rows mean no JSON.Obj run, not a loss. In the library chart fast-json-parse wraps JSON.parse, which is why it equals native JSON (547 MB/s). The SIMD mode is slower than SWAR on several deserialize rows (Small Payload 1,089 vs 2,196 MB/s). A key-matching correctness bug (final UTF-16 unit of odd-length keys longer than 4 units not compared) was fixed on 2026-10-04 (PR #223), after the charted run; the fix is in toMemCCheck/toMemCDecl, which only the generated __DESERIALIZE_SLOW fallback uses, and the AS large bench asserts a byte-exact round trip, so the charted fast-path numbers are not capped by it. Charts dated Jul 17 2026 (commit 0bb47d4); main has moved to 1.6.1 since.

notes: Every claimed figure matches the charts: deserialize SWAR vs built-in JSON 1,321 vs 568 (1.1 kB), 5,734 vs 1,295 (5.5 kB), 2,196 vs 168 (108 B), 1,056 vs 401 MB/s (52 B); serialize SIMD 7,775 vs 1,062 and 3,818 vs 696 MB/s; library chart 5,636 vs 547 MB/s; 3D Vector 356-444 vs 83 and JSON.Obj 82 vs 83. Metadata: MIT, 113 stars, not a fork, last commit 2026-10-05 (active). Shortcomings to record: per-op eval in the JS harness only, typed-struct vs generic-object work, lazy JSON.Obj bars, unchecked builds (--noAssert, -tnh), first-party.

tier_reason: The README chart (doc/benchmark.png) and doc/benchmark-results.pdf compare Speedy.js with the same code run as plain JS in Chrome and Firefox, and the harness is public (packages/benchmark/run-benchmarks.js on benchmark.js, cases/*.ts, *-spdy.ts, *.cc, compile-emcc), but no CPU model is stated anywhere (the results/*.json files record only an Intel Mac OS X 10.12.5 browser user agent) and Speedy.js compile options are defaults, so not A. The VMIL 2017 paper could not be opened (splashcon, sigplan.org, ost.ch and orix.ost.ch all failed DNS here); only a search-snippet abstract ('up to four times faster') was seen, so per the snippet-only precedent (Instrew, rv32emu) the entry stays C until someone reads the paper, which would likely make it B.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Speedy.js: speedyjs-loader 0.0.19 with default compiler options (LLVM WebAssembly backend, TypeScript fork 2.3.3-with-int); flags not stated. Emscripten comparison: em++ -O3 -std=c++11 -s BINARYEN_PASSES='post-emscripten' -s INVOKE_RUN=0 -s ALLOW_MEMORY_GROWTH=1 (packages/benchmark/cases/compile-emcc). Harness: benchmark.js ^2.1.4 driven by packages/benchmark/run-benchmarks.js in the browser.
corrections.hardware: Not stated; packages/benchmark/results/*.json record only the browser user agent (e.g. Chrome 59 on Intel Mac OS X 10.12.5), no CPU model.
corrections.claimed_speedup: README chart doc/benchmark.png (speedup vs the same code as JS, 100% = equal), Chrome 58.0.3029.110: fib 352%, isPrime 311%, nsieve 273%, mergeSortInt 140%, tspInt 134%, mergeSort 124%, simjs 113%, intCompare 108%, tspArrayInt 107%, doubleCompare 102%, doubleAdd 100%, tspArrayDouble 100%, tspDouble 100%, arrayReverse 91%. Firefox 53.0: arrayReverse 444%, nsieve 399%, fib 288%, mergeSortInt 167%, mergeSort 157%, tspInt 138%, simjs 133%, tspArrayInt 112%, isPrime 106%, tspArrayDouble 97%, doubleAdd 96%, doubleCompare 96%, intCompare 94%, tspDouble 98%. A separate run in doc/benchmark-results.pdf (Table 1, ops/s, browser versions not given) gives, Chrome / Firefox (derived from page data): fib 3.42x / 3.0x, isPrime 3.23x / 1.07x, nsieve 1.99x / 4.03x, arrayReverse 1.02x / 4.64x, tspInt 1.37x / 1.41x, mergeSort 1.30x / 1.55x, simjs 1.08x / 1.22x, tspDouble 1.0x / 0.98x. The VMIL 2017 abstract (search snippet only) says up to four times faster and run-time fluctuation halved.
corrections.caveats: First-party numbers from 2017 engines (Chrome 58/59, Firefox 53); no CPU model, Speedy.js compile options unstated. Peer-reviewed basis, Reiser and Blaeser, 'Accelerate JavaScript Applications by Cross-Compiling to WebAssembly', VMIL 2017, was not opened (only an abstract snippet), so tier C pending paper access. Mixed result: about half the kernels are at or below parity (arrayReverse 91% in Chrome, intCompare 94%, doubleAdd 96%, doubleCompare 96%, tspDouble 98% in Firefox), and the README chart and the PDF table are different runs with different ratios (e.g. Chrome nsieve 273% vs 1.99x). Speedy.js accepts only a restricted, typed JavaScript subset and needs a custom TypeScript fork and an LLVM build with the experimental WebAssembly target. Archived 2023-04-22; the author calls it very experimental.

notes: Downgrade B to C: the chart numbers in the record are accurate, but the only peer-reviewed source (VMIL 2017) was unreachable and seen only as a snippet, and the repo methodology lacks a CPU model. Added the doc/benchmark-results.pdf table (derived ratios) and the Emscripten build flags from compile-emcc. Metadata: MIT, 342 stars, archived 2023-04-22, last commit 2017-10-23 (abandoned). A retier to B is possible if someone reads the VMIL paper.
